actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: Uranoscopus scaber is widespread in the Eastern Atlantic, including the Mediterranean and Black seas, and also occurs in the Red Sea. In the Northeastern Atlantic, this species occurs from the bay of Biscay to Portugal and throughout the Mediterranean and Black seas. This species has been confirmed from Mauritania, but cannot yet be confirmed from Senegal (Tito de Morais pers. comm. 2014). This species is found at depths ranging from 15–400 m (Roux 1990).
documentation.population:
Uranoscopus scaber is most abundant during the spring/summer period (Demirhan et al. 2007). This species is considered common off the coasts of Europe and Africa, and is very common in the Mediterranean (Çoker et al. 2008).

Off the Egyptian Mediterranean coast, the population was characterized by a low exploitation rate (Rizkalla et al. 2009). Off the southeastern Black Sea, the total length of this species ranged from 5.2 to 21.9 cm, and the population was composed of five age-classes. The population was composed of 32.94% male, 65.31% female (Demirhan et al. 2007). In the Northern Aegean Sea, U. scaber ranged in size from 8.7 to 26.9 cm (Karachle and Stergiou 2008). The maximum size of this species is 40 cm, however it is more commonly seen to 30 cm. Subpopulations in the Black Sea, where this species is not typically commercially utilized but is taken as bycatch, are seen to a maximum size of 21.9 cm. MEDITS survey shows fluctuations in abundance from 1993 to 2010. Survey data from the IBTS Gulf of Cadiz also shows fluctuations from 1993 to 2013
documentation.habitats:
Uranoscopus scaber is found buried in sand and mud of the continental shelf and upper slope, between 15 and about 400 metres depth. It feeds primarily on fishes. It reaches a maximum size of 40 cm, and is more common to 30 cm. Mature males are often about 14 cm. In a study focusing on differences among fish assemblages associated with a variety of habitats in the Adriatic Sea, U. scaber was found exclusively over unvegetated sand habitats (Guidetti 2000). In the Black Sea, the sex ratio was biased toward females (1:1.98). The population was composed of five age-classes. Spawning in the Aegean sea occurs from March to September (Çoker et al. 2006). The diet consists of small crabs and fish (Papoutsoglou and Lyndon 2003). In Egyptian Mediterranean waters, females reach larger sizes than males, attaining 30 cm while males are typically seen at 26 cm (Rizkalla and Bakhoum 2009).

Uranoscopids occur in littoral areas and waters of the continental shelf and slope to depths of 400 metres. All species are bottom-dwelling, usually burrowing in sandy or muddy sediments leaving only their eyes exposed. They are carnivorous ambush predators. Some species are electric, though they are unlikely to be strong enough to be harmful to humans. The sharp humeral spine is venomous (Smith in press).
documentation.threats: There have been no confirmed population declines in U. scaber. It is taken as bycatch in a number of fisheries, and is commercially important off the Mediterranean coast of Egypt.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for U. cadenati. Its distribution overlaps with several marine protected areas (MPAs). In the western Mediterranean, off coasts of Spain and France, there are three MPAs that are over 20 years old and have varying restrictions. Catches were done by trammel nets. Uranoscopus scaber was found to increase in intermediate distance catches. A decreasing trend with distance from MPA was also found but only during one season (Forcada et al. 2009).
documentation.use_trade: Uranoscopus scaber is collected mainly with bottom trawls and is marketed fresh and dried-salted (Smith in press). It has no economic value in the Black Sea (Demirhan et al. 2007); however it is commercially important in Egypt, and there are plans to manage the fishery in this region (Rizkalla and Bakhoum 2009). It is rarely found in the commercial catches from the eastern part of the Egyptian Mediterranean coast, whereas it constitutes 2.6% of trawl catch from the western Egyptian Mediterranean coast (El-Sayes et al. 2001). It is discarded from commercial purse seine vessels in the Aegean and Ionian seas (Tsagarakis et al. 2012). Uranoscopus scaber is a component of artisanal fisheries in the Tyrrhenian Sea. Here, it is taken in trammel and combined nets for cuttlefish and red mullets (Collaca et al. 2004). In the Black Sea, U. scaber is captured predominantly as bycatch, and is most abundant during the spring/summer period (Demirhan et al. 2007)
documentation.rationale: Uranoscopus scaber is widespread in the Mediterranean and Black seas as well as along the Atlantic coast of Europe up to Portugal and the Bay of Biscay. It is known from Morocco, with reports of the species being collected along the African coast down to Senegal. It is found at depths ranging from 15 to 400 metres. It appears to be common in the Mediterranean and Black Seas, however there is little information concerning its abundance off the western coast of Africa. It is commercially utilized in some parts of its range, and discarded in others. There are no species-specific threats to U. scaber, however it is likely impacted by trawling in parts of its range. There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for U. scaber, however its distribution overlaps with some marine protected areas. This species is assessed as Least Concern.
